PAGE / FOLIO: [29] (recto) | IIIF Canvas #7 (b18775275_MS_990_0007.JP2)
Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0007.JP2#xywh=240,314,4537,6150
Summary:      First extant text page of the Arzneibuch ([p. 29], recto preceding p. 30; pages 1–28 wanting). Written in double column within red rules with red rubrics. Contains iatrochemical and folk-medical recipes using eggshells (for urinary calculus, hemorrhage, proud flesh), chimney soot (for cancer and plague anthrax), and sourdough bread (pharmacological properties, maturing poultice, febrile headache, inflamed eyes, post-febrile halitosis, and sustaining life by the aroma of bread).

[p29_colA_l01]         (#xywh=240,314,2416,154)   {rubric: For sand and stone [urinary gravel and calculus].}  // Note: Red rubric; upper right margin of col. A slightly abraded.
[p29_colA_l02]         (#xywh=240,468,2416,154)   Take [℞] the eggshells from which young chicks have hatched  // Note: ℞ = Recipe.
[p29_colA_l03]         (#xywh=240,622,2416,153)   out, remove the soft white inner membrane,  // Note: hienlen = Hühnlein (chicks); häutl = Häutlein.
[p29_colA_l04]         (#xywh=240,775,2416,154)   make the shells into powder [ꝑll̵], and take 1 drachm [ℨj]  // Note: ꝑll̵ = Pulver (powder); ℨj = 1 drachm.
[p29_colA_l05]         (#xywh=240,929,2416,154)   in wine [V̈]; it is a precious remedy against sand,  // Note: V̈ = Vinum / Wein.
[p29_colA_l06]         (#xywh=240,1083,2416,153)  stone, and obstructed urine [⊡].  // Note: ⊡ = Urina / Harn (strangury / urinary retention).
[p29_colA_l07]         (#xywh=240,1236,2416,154)  Others take any eggshell and strip out
[p29_colA_l08]         (#xywh=240,1390,2416,154)  the white [inner lining] from it.
[p29_colA_l09]         (#xywh=240,1544,2416,154)  {rubric: To staunch blood [Hemostasis].}  // Note: Red rubric.
[p29_colA_l10]         (#xywh=240,1698,2416,154)  Take [℞] and soak eggshells in vinegar [✚] until they become  // Note: ✚ = Acetum / Essig (vinegar).
[p29_colA_l11]         (#xywh=240,1852,2416,153)  soft; afterwards dry them in the sun [☉] and make them  // Note: ☉ = Sol / Sonne.
[p29_colA_l12]         (#xywh=240,2005,2416,154)  into powder [ꝑll̵], and strew it upon a hemorrhage, wherever
[p29_colA_l13]         (#xywh=240,2159,2416,154)  it may be, and it staunches it immediately.  // Note: von stund an = instantaneously.
[p29_colA_l14]         (#xywh=240,2313,2416,153)  The shells alone calcined to powder [✗] and strewed upon  // Note: ✗ = calcined powder / lime.
[p29_colA_l15]         (#xywh=240,2466,2416,154)  bleeding hemorrhoids [fließende goldene Ader] stops the flow.  // Note: gulden ader = vena aurea (hemorrhoidal vein).
[p29_colA_l16]         (#xywh=240,2620,2416,154)  For the inflamed male member, boil egg-
[p29_colA_l17]         (#xywh=240,2774,2416,154)  shells and clay in good white wine [V̈], and foment  // Note: bahe = bathe/foment (warm compress).
[p29_colA_l18]         (#xywh=240,2928,2416,154)  yourself therewith, and you will experience wonders.
[p29_colA_l19]         (#xywh=240,3082,2416,153)  {rubric: Cauterizing [Escharotic].} Burn eggshells in the furnace until they turn  // Note: Inline red rubric 'Özen' (= Ätzen).
[p29_colA_l20]         (#xywh=240,3235,2416,154)  white; this powder [ꝑll̵] serves for eating away  // Note: Quicklime (CaO) produced by calcining eggshells.
[p29_colA_l21]         (#xywh=240,3389,2416,154)  proud flesh [exuberant granulation tissue].  // Note: wildes Fleisch = caro luxurians.
[p29_colA_l22]         (#xywh=240,3543,2416,153)  {rubric: For cancer [ulcerated carcinoma / phagedenic ulcer] —}  // Note: Red rubric.
[p29_colA_l23]         (#xywh=240,3696,2416,154)  Take [℞] soot out of the chimney, wine-lees,  // Note: wain leger = Weinleger (wine lees / tartar).
[p29_colA_l24]         (#xywh=240,3850,2416,154)  iron rust, [and] goat's cheese; make out of them all a
[p29_colA_l25]         (#xywh=240,4004,2416,154)  plaster, lay it over the cancer for 48 hours,
[p29_colA_l26]         (#xywh=240,4158,2416,154)  and the cancer dies, or at the very least one

[p29_colA_l29]         (#xywh=240,4619,2416,154)  {rubric: Plague.} In the plague, {del: the aforesaid} {add: the following} plaster is  // Note: Inline red rubric 'Pöß.' (= Pest); 'obgemeltes' struck through.
[p29_colA_l30]         (#xywh=240,4773,2416,153)  a glorious remedy for the carbuncle [anthrax]: Take  // Note: antrax = plague carbuncle / bubo.
[p29_colA_l31]         (#xywh=240,4926,2416,154)  the hard soot out of the chimney, 10 ounces [℥x],
[p29_colA_l32]         (#xywh=240,5080,2416,154)  sourdough, turpentine, and butter, of each 1 ounce [āā ℥j],  // Note: āā = ana (of each an equal quantity).
[p29_colA_l33]         (#xywh=240,5234,2416,154)  Venetian soap 1½ ounces [℥iß], 3 egg yolks,

[p29_colA_l36]         (#xywh=240,5695,2416,154)  {rubric: Virtue of sourdough —}  // Note: Red rubric.
[p29_colA_l37]         (#xywh=240,5849,2416,154)  Sourdough possesses a mixed [galenic] quality
[p29_colA_l38]         (#xywh=240,6003,2416,153)  of a temperate warmth and of cooling,
[p29_colA_l39]         (#xywh=240,6156,2416,154)  such that it neither cools too much nor heats
[p29_colA_l40]         (#xywh=240,6310,2416,154)  too much; it resolves, ripens [matures], and also [serves] to  // Note: Continues across column break to col. B, l. 1 ('waichen'). Quire mark '2.' below.

[p29_colB_l14]         (#xywh=2656,2264,2121,150) apply it afresh.
[p29_colB_l15]         (#xywh=2656,2414,2121,150) Sourdough mixed with salt [🜔] and oil softens
[p29_colB_l16]         (#xywh=2656,2564,2121,150) pestilential pustules and hard

[p29_colB_l18]         (#xywh=2656,2864,2121,150) Sourdough mixed with sharp lye
[p29_colB_l19]         (#xywh=2656,3014,2121,150) and laid over putrid ulcers draws out all
[p29_colB_l20]         (#xywh=2656,3164,2121,150) impurity.
[p29_colB_l21]         (#xywh=2656,3314,2121,150) {rubric: Inflamed eyes.} Take [℞] bread of rye  // Note: Inline red rubric 'Erhizte augen.'
[p29_colB_l22]         (#xywh=2656,3464,2121,150) or wheat, steep it in rose-water [▽] [and]

[p29_colB_l24]         (#xywh=2656,3764,2121,150) out a little, and bind it over the inflamed
[p29_colB_l25]         (#xywh=2656,3914,2121,150) eyes.
[p29_colB_l26]         (#xywh=2656,4064,2121,150) {rubric: Fetid breath [halitosis] after an illness}  // Note: Red rubric.
[p29_colB_l27]         (#xywh=2656,4214,2121,150) When after a fever or other illness
[p29_colB_l28]         (#xywh=2656,4364,2121,150) the mouth smells foul, take cold  // Note: Austro-Bavarian 'schmäkht' = smells/stinks.

Contains recipes for colic (Grimen), stiffening of the nerves (Nerven Erstarrung), pleurisy (Seiden stechen), plague prophylaxis (Pöß), the folk pediatric 'heart-worm or goat-worm' tested via a live gudgeon fish bound to the navel (Gaiß Würm den khindern), joint-water discharge (Glidt Wasser), consumption (Dörsucht / Dörsichtigen), snail oil for wasted limbs (Schwinden der glider), cough and hemoptysis (Hüesten vnd außwurff), and plague/poisoned wounds.

Summary:      Page 32 (recto, numbered '32' in upper-right margin; faces p. 30 on verso Canvas 8, skipping '31' in pagination without text loss). Column A completes the recipe from p. 30, then gives an important historical note on Balsam of Copaiba ('Balsamo Copauia') recently imported from the Indies ('auß India') and used for remarkable cures in Vienna ('in Wienn' — confirming the manuscript's Austrian provenance), followed by surgical management of carious jawbone (incision, actual cautery, oil of vitriol, exfoliation) and syringe-injections for dental fistulae. Column B features a half-column watercolour bust portrait of a mustachioed gentleman in a red doublet and wide pleated ruff, above remedies for putrefaction/ulceration of the mouth ('Von fälung des Mundts', stomatitis/scurvy), including a pauper's remedy ('arme leüd die nichts Vermögen') of watercress, scurvy-grass, and horseradish.

PAGE / FOLIO: 33 (verso) | IIIF Canvas #10 (b18775275_MS_990_0010.JP2)
Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0010.JP2#xywh=528,368,4553,6163
Summary:      Page 33 (verso, numbered '33' in upper-left margin). Column A treats scraping necrotic gum roots with a razor ('schar mäser'), incarnative powders to make rotted gums grow back, tightening loose teeth ('Zant wagel'), a potent sublimate-and-alum water applied with a small screw/swab, and remedies for halitosis. Column B treats inflammation and swelling of the tonsils and uvula ('Mandl vnd Zäpffel'), including lead acetate ('bleÿ Zukher') gargles and the folk-surgical maneuver of pulling the patient hard by the earlobes to raise a fallen uvula ('Wan das Zäpffel abgefallen ziehe ihm Woll beÿ den ohr läpel'), followed by a watercolour drawing of four multi-rooted human molar teeth and the opening of the treatise on toothache ('Von den Zänten Zuestänten vnd khrankheiten').

Distinguishes hot vs. cold catarrhal fluxions, observes that extraction ('herauß reiß') is the only permanent cure for carious teeth, and provides anodyne cotton-wool pellets, aural instillation of castoreum or horseradish juice, temporal plasters (Gum Elemi, mastic, opium), Laudanum opiatum, camphor ('XXX'), guaiacum-wine solar digests, and astrological/solar remedies using ash-wood ('lign. fraxino') gathered on St. John's Day (Midsummer) before sunrise ('Vor auf gang der ☉') and sorrel gathered in June before sunrise.

Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0012.JP2#xywh=211,243,4978,6312
Summary:      Page 35 (verso, numbered '35' in upper-left margin). Column A covers remedies for carious teeth, non-surgical chemical shedding of rotten teeth ('Das die Zant auß falen') using mulberry root steeped in strong vinegar, tooth-preserving and whitening powders (burnt hartshorn, mastic, calcined salt), and infant teething remedies ('Das den khindern die Zant Paldt Wachsen') using butter, honey, and hare's brain ('hasen hirn') rubbed on the gums ('Zant Piller'). Column B opens with a watercolour illustration of a spotted frog ('Fröschel')—a visual pun on sublingual ranula ('Von Fröschel vnder der Zungen / ranula', literally 'little frog')—followed by medical and surgical treatment of ranula (astringent gargles, lancet incision, or venesection of the sublingual vein).

PAGE / FOLIO: 39 (20r) | IIIF Canvas #16 (b18775275_MS_990_0016.JP2)
Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0016.JP2#xywh=208,236,4886,6298
Summary:      Page 39 (fol. 20r) continues the treatise on Angina, distinguishing true 'Angina exquisita' (with high fever, thirst, and mortal danger of suffocation) from 'Angina spuria' (false angina). It provides prognostic signs ('NB: Pronostico') and outlines the urgent therapeutic regimen ('Die Chur'), emphasizing immediate clysters, repeated bloodletting (median vein, leeches, sublingual veins), and warm foot/arm baths.

PAGE / FOLIO: 49 (verso) | IIIF Canvas #26 (b18775275_MS_990_0026.JP2)
Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0026.JP2#xywh=688,274,4643,6271
Summary:      Page 49 (verso, numbered '49' in upper-left margin; full-width single-column layout across the red-ruled frame, cited in Wellcome catalogue 'Pp. 49-165 are devoted to ophthalmology'). Completes the sentence from p. 48 col. B l. 53 ('genand Cornea'), then treats: (1) The Three Humors of the Eye (Vitreus, Crystallinus, Albugineus/Aquosus, noting that cataract arises in the anterior aqueous humor); (2) The Six Extraocular Muscles (noting the Vesalian observation that the 7th retractor bulbi muscle exists only in beasts/cattle and not in humans); and (3) A scholastic Latin-German synthesis of the parts, nerves, vessels, glands, and tunics constituting the eye.

### [49 — Full-Width Text Block (within red rules X=688..5331, Y=274..6545)]

[p49_full_l01]         (#xywh=688,274,4643,143)   [49 |] called Cornea. Finally there is yet another membrane, which takes its first origin from the  // Note: Completes sentence from p. 48, col. B, l. 53.
[p49_full_l02]         (#xywh=688,417,4643,142)   hard membrane pericranium; therefrom springs the outermost pellicle, called the Conjunctiva,
[p49_full_l03]         (#xywh=688,559,4643,143)   which is the white in the eye, and has its connection with the 6 muscles that move the
[p49_full_l04]         (#xywh=688,702,4643,142)   eyes. —
[p49_full_l05]         (#xywh=688,844,4643,143)   {rubric: Of the Three Humors of the Eyes}  // Note: Centered red rubric.
[p49_full_l06]         (#xywh=688,987,4643,142)   Within the eyes are enclosed 3 humors by which the eyes are filled, which are variously
[p49_full_l07]         (#xywh=688,1129,4643,143)  named as follows: 1. Vitreus. 2. Crystallinus. 3. Albugineus. The posterior humor,
[p49_full_l08]         (#xywh=688,1272,4643,142)  namely the Vitreus, is embraced from behind by the membrane retina. — The second humor,
[p49_full_l09]         (#xywh=688,1414,4643,143)  the Crystallinus [lens], lies in the middle of the eye; it is of the size of a pea, yet not completely round,  // Note: erbes = Erbse (pea).
[p49_full_l10]         (#xywh=688,1557,4643,142)  but somewhat flattened [lenticular], especially on the posterior part toward the Vitreus; this is neither truly hard
[p49_full_l11]         (#xywh=688,1699,4643,143)  nor truly soft, in colour like a white sapphire or frozen ice, yet somewhat
[p49_full_l12]         (#xywh=688,1842,4643,142)  yellowish. This humor, together with the anterior part of the Vitreus, is covered over by the membrane
[p49_full_l13]         (#xywh=688,1984,4643,143)  aranea, which separates the humor albugineus from the other two.
[p49_full_l14]         (#xywh=688,2127,4643,142)  The third humor lies in the anterior part of the eye [and] is called albugineus aquosus [aqueous humor]. This
[p49_full_l15]         (#xywh=688,2269,4643,143)  humor is surrounded by the membrane Uvea up to the aperture [pupil], and thereafter the Cornea retains it;
[p49_full_l16]         (#xywh=688,2412,4643,142)  in this anterior humor arise the Cataracta, the couching-cataract [Star].  // Note: Classical Galenic/medieval locus of cataract as a suffusion in the aqueous chamber.
[p49_full_l17]         (#xywh=688,2554,4643,143)  {rubric: Of the Muscles of the Eyes}  // Note: Centered red rubric.
[p49_full_l18]         (#xywh=688,2697,4643,142)  The eye has 6 muscles [musculi]: the 1st which draws the eye upward; the 2nd which draws the eye downward;
[p49_full_l19]         (#xywh=688,2839,4643,143)  the 3rd which draws the eye upward toward the side; the 4th which draws the eye downward toward the side. Thereafter
[p49_full_l20]         (#xywh=688,2982,4643,142)  there are 2 further muscles: one that draws the eye toward the great [medial] canthus, and one that draws it toward the
[p49_full_l21]         (#xywh=688,3124,4643,143)  lesser [lateral] canthus. There are also other authors who insist upon a 7th muscle which
[p49_full_l22]         (#xywh=688,3267,4643,143)  surrounds the nervus opticus [retractor bulbi], which however is found only in the eyes of beasts/cattle, whereas in  // Note: Vesalius (Fabrica, 1543) refuted Galen's 7th human eye muscle as an ungulate/bovine structure.
[p49_full_l23]         (#xywh=688,3410,4643,142)  human eyes only 6 muscles are found. —
[p49_full_l24]         (#xywh=688,3552,4643,143)  {rubric: Follows Further concerning the Eyes and Their Parts, How They Are by God}  // Note: Red rubric.
[p49_full_l25]         (#xywh=688,3695,4643,142)  {rubric: Created and Joined Together}  // Note: Red rubric with ornamental flourish.
[p49_full_l26]         (#xywh=688,3837,4643,143)  There exists among the oculists a controversy regarding the parts or tunics of the eyes:
[p49_full_l27]         (#xywh=688,3980,4643,142)  and some wish to maintain there are only 2 tunics, others insist on 3, others will have
[p49_full_l28]         (#xywh=688,4122,4643,143)  4, others 5 or 6; the majority, however, agree and speak of seven
[p49_full_l29]         (#xywh=688,4265,4643,142)  tunics.
[p49_full_l30]         (#xywh=688,4407,4643,143)  These tunics are named in the following manner: first the Conjunctiva, Cornea,
[p49_full_l31]         (#xywh=688,4550,4643,142)  Uvea, Aranea, Retiformis, and Vitrea; the dura or sclerotica is a part of the Cornea,
[p49_full_l32]         (#xywh=688,4692,4643,143)  {del: [cancelled in red: et Uvea]}, the interstitium ciliare is a part of the Uvea, the pupilla is the  // Note: Two words at left of l. 32 obliterated by a thick red bar.
[p49_full_l33]         (#xywh=688,4835,4643,142)  little aperture in the front of the Uvea; the Iris is also a part of the Uvea.
[p49_full_l34]         (#xywh=688,4977,4643,143)  Beyond this there are also in the eye three humores, namely aquosus, crystallinus, and
[p49_full_l35]         (#xywh=688,5120,4643,142)  vitreus. To the constitution of the eye come together: the nervus opticus, spiritus
[p49_full_l36]         (#xywh=688,5262,4643,143)  visivus atque facultas visiva [visual spirit and visual faculty], where there is also some fat, adeps; there are
[p49_full_l37]         (#xywh=688,5405,4643,142)  also several small nerves from the second pair [ex secunda coniugatione], the two canthi [anguli duo], also the caruncula  // Note: Galenic 2nd pair of cranial nerves = oculomotor nerve.
[p49_full_l38]         (#xywh=688,5547,4643,143)  lacrimalis, as well as two glandulae [lacrimal glands]; beyond this belong to the eyes the super-
[p49_full_l39]         (#xywh=688,5690,4643,142)  cilia [eyebrows] and the orbita itself, and all this besides the arteriae and venae.

Summary:      Page 53 (verso, numbered '53' in upper-left margin). Column A enumerates six internal and external causes of cataracts (brain, phlegmatic blood, foul stomach/spleen/liver vapors, coarse foods like onions, garlic, horseradish, mustard, smoked meat, peas, and lentils, excessive weeping, and trauma), and refutes the common belief that a cataract must take 7 years to ripen, citing the author's own clinical experience curing patients blind for only 6 months to 2 years. Column B lists the prodromal signs of cataract ('Von den Zaichen des Staan': cobwebs, floaters/flies, nets, fog, colored halos, diplopia, congenital cataract) and explains how to distinguish gastric vs. cranial origin ('die Vrsach Zuerkhenen ob sÿe Seÿ auß dem Magen oder haubt') by fluctuation with meals, time of day, lunar phase, and weather. Column A describes positioning the patient facing a window on a stool, the oculist facing him with the patient's hands resting on the oculist's knees, an assistant holding the head against his chest, bandaging the sound eye, using the right hand for the left eye and left hand for the right eye, parting the eyelids, and inserting the needle 1.5 knife-backs from the cornea through the conjunctiva. Column B details passing behind the uvea without touching the crystalline lens, depressing the cataract into the lower vitreous, holding it down for 2 or 3 Paternosters ('2 od[er] 3 Vatter Vnser'), withdrawing the needle, and managing a rising or tough/adherent cataract. Transcribed with Gemini 4.
Model:        Gemini 4

Summary:      Page 78 (recto, numbered '78' in upper-right margin; pagination jumps from 75 to 78 without textual loss). Column A opens Complication 4 ('der 4 Zuefall. Wan grosse Schmerzen in die augen khumen') and analyzes three causes of severe post-operative pain ('Woher Soliche Schmerzen khumen'): (1) inexperienced oculists using thick, unpolished needles that let the vitreous humor escape; (2) improper piercing and overly tight bandaging; (3) cold drafts entering the eye before healing. Column B adds emotional/environmental triggers (anger, fright, weeping, wind, smoke, sleeplessness, hard stools) and prescribes 'Mitel Vor grosse Reisen vnd Wehe tag des haubts' (senna-tamarind purge) and 'Ein anders Purgier Tränckhel' followed by cephalic venesection and vesicatoria behind the ears. Transcribed with Gemini 4.

PAGE / FOLIO: 82 (recto) | IIIF Canvas #53 (b18775275_MS_990_0053.JP2)
Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0053.JP2#xywh=180,180,4700,6340
Summary:      Page 82 (recto, numbered '82' in upper-right margin). Column A prescribes purgation, vesicatoria, 'Ain guette Lattwerung Züe den aufgestignen Starn', and 'Ain guettes Wasser Zü disen Zuefall', then opens the major treatise on Lacrimal Fistula ('Von den fistlen der augen — fistula Lacrimale'), describing how smallpox or salty humors ulcerate the inner canthus and erode the lacrimal bone (os lacrimale / caries). Column B warns that chirurgians who fail to treat lacrimal fistulae carefully risk great harm, explains how pressing a finger at the inner canthus beside the nose expresses white/purulent matter ('weisse vnd häutige materj'), and displays a half-column watercolour portrait of a nun in a black veil and white wimple pressing her finger to a weeping, blood-streaked lacrimal fistula in her right inner canthus, concluding that the surest cure is incision and actual cautery. Transcribed with Gemini 4.

Summary:      Page 87 (verso, numbered '87' in upper-left margin). Opens the alternative surgical method for lacrimal fistula: trephining/perforating the lacrimal bone ('Es ist noch ein andere Weiß vnd manier die augen fistel Zü Churieren. Namblich durch das perforieren oder durch born'). Column A details pre-operative accumulation of pus for 3–4 days, bandaging the sound eye, incising down to the bone, and widening with sponge tents. Column B describes perforating the 'os cribrum' (ethmoid/lacrimal bone) with the spiral-tipped bone drill shown in Figure '#.o 6.' ('Form vnd gestalt der Jnstrument Zum durch born'), illustrating three slender metal drills with auger tips and turned wooden handles. Transcribed with Gemini 4.

Column B displays a watercolour of three gleaming brass/gold basins on a shelf ('fig_p103_three_brass_vessels'), followed by 'Ain anders für augen hiz vnd Rötte' (sugar of lead, alum-egg) and an important clinical 'NB' warning oculists to distinguish cold fluxes (requiring warm steamings/baths) from hot salty fluxes (requiring cooling, bloodletting, and purging). Transcribed with Gemini 4.

(bust wearing a yellow-orange patterned cap and dark-rimmed spectacles). Below Portrait .M., the text classifies eye colors (black as strongest, blue as weakest yet loveliest, grey as nimble) and eye sizes (small eyes sharper than large protruding eyes). Column B warns against delaying treatment ('Sight is the highest treasure, yet people often treat their eyes as if they had more eyes than fingers on their hand') and gives 'Ein khöstliches Pulver Zü stärkhen aines Schwachen gesicht' and 'Ein Arcana das gesicht Zü Stärkh[en]'.

PAGE / FOLIO: 119 (verso) | IIIF Canvas #90 (b18775275_MS_990_0090.JP2)
Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0090.JP2#xywh=360,180,4780,6320
Summary:      Page 119 (verso, numbered '119' in upper-left margin). Column A concludes the etiology of white (melancholic) and yellow (bilious) purulent eye fluxes, prescribing purgation with species dia turbith or cochia/aureae pills, shoulder/nape cupping, and venesection, followed by two eye-bag poultices ('Ein guetes Säckhel auf die augen für aitern vnd Schweren') and two distilled waters ('Ein Guetes Waser für aitern vnd Schweren der augen'). Column B gives two ointments ('Ein Guetes Sälbel für das aitern der augen'), 'Ein guetes Puluer vnd Pflaster in den süren flüß', and opens the new chapter 'Stöchen vnd drükhen der augen' (gritty/sandy sensation from hot humors, blisters, or engorged veins in the conjunctiva).
Model:        Gemini 4

[p121_left_l01]        (#xywh=380,180,2540,150)   121.  // Note: Original page number in a ruled box at top left.

[p121_left_l04]        (#xywh=380,630,2540,150)   The heat-blisters come from these causes,  // Note: Vrsach for Ursachen.
[p121_left_l05]        (#xywh=380,780,2540,150)   as previously mentioned, from the heat
[p121_left_l06]        (#xywh=380,930,2540,150)   and irritation of the eyes, namely from superfluous  // Note: vd = vnd (und); kizlen = itching/irritation.
[p121_left_l07]        (#xywh=380,1080,2540,150)  saline humor of the brain and of the

[p121_left_l11]        (#xywh=380,1680,2540,150)  that such people, with great heat of the eyes  // Note: leidt = Leute (people).
[p121_left_l12]        (#xywh=380,1830,2540,150)  and stinging, have redness [and] watering of the eyes,
[p121_left_l13]        (#xywh=380,1980,2540,150)  also often cannot endure the light. Some  // Note: ach = auch; khin = können (photophobia).
[p121_left_l14]        (#xywh=380,2130,2540,150)  little blisters are at first very small and white
[p121_left_l15]        (#xywh=380,2280,2540,150)  on the outside, as large as a poppy seed. Afterwards  // Note: mogen khorn = Mohnkorn (poppy seed).

[p121_left_l18]        (#xywh=380,2730,2540,150)  the wider out, and often cover over the entire  // Note: Reading of 'über ziehn' somewhat compressed in Kurrent.
[p121_left_l19]        (#xywh=380,2880,2540,150)  eyeball. Some sink in, and make a  // Note: ein [fallen/sinken] or ain.
[p121_left_l20]        (#xywh=380,3030,2540,150)  little pit in the cornea. And if one  // Note: Corneal ulceration.
[p121_left_l21]        (#xywh=380,3180,2540,150)  neglects it, it eats away the cornea so far that  // Note: vber sicht = übersieht (neglects).

Summary:      Recto folio (p. 134) in a two-column layout detailing the third surgical cure for trichiasis ('Die drite Chur ist. die har sambt den fleisch Hinwegh Zue Schneiden'), involving suturing and excising the eyelid margin, followed by post-operative poultice/plaster care using egg white and a mineral/gold-marked ingredient, a warning to operate while the patient is fasting, and a powder recipe for proud flesh ('Ein Puluer Zum überigen fleisch'). Summary:      Page 195 (verso) of Wellcome Collection MS.990 contains early modern German and Latin medical recipes for treating quartan and tertian fevers. The left column presents a complex electuary ('Die Lattwerung mach also') incorporating aromatic roots, herbs, hartshorn, coral, seeds, honey, and Peruvian bark (cinchona), followed by detailed German dosing and regimen instructions. PAGE / FOLIO: 398 (recto) | IIIF Canvas #169 (b18775275_MS_990_0169.JP2)
Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0169.JP2#xywh=300,300,4904,6253
Summary:      A folio from a late 17th-century German medical manuscript (Wellcome MS.990, p. 398) discussing contagious fevers ('Contagios oder anfengig'). The text describes how pestilential poisons enter the body through air, food, drink, breath, stench, or fear, attacking the heart and brain. It provides preventive measures including fumigation with juniper wood, masterwort, and lovage, along with purgation, bloodletting, and several compound recipes (an electuary with theriac, Armenian bole, and alkermes; pills with myrrh, gum ammoniac, and aloes; and a 'famous poison powder' of valerian, swallowwort, polypody, lovage, angelica, and herb Paris). The final section addresses the cure of the fever, noting its severity as a divine punishment requiring repentance before natural remedies, and warning physicians that deceptive pulses and urine signs can mask the illness.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Tokens Used:  Input: 1,600 | Output: 2,850

Summary:      Folio 99 verso of Wellcome Collection MS.990 (c. 1675) continues a treatise on pestilential fever and its treatment. The left column outlines the fivefold (headed '4 weg') therapeutic regimen—air correction, vomitives, purgation via the bowels, sweating, and tempering of heat and cold—followed by diagnostic signs of acute thirst, precordial oppression, and shivering, and introduces a protective fumigation ('Rauch') accompanied by an illustration of a smoking censer. The right column provides the compound fumigation recipe (including olibanum, amber, myrrh, mastic, asa foetida, hartshorn, angelica, pimpernel, and spun hemp, silk, gold, and silver threads) and a section on therapeutic vomiting ('Yber brechen in disen fieber') illustrated by a man vomiting into a tub, recommending mild emetics such as linseed, walnut, or bitter almond oil, hazelwort with oxymel, and a feather dipped in scorpion oil.

PAGE / FOLIO: 208 (recto) | IIIF Canvas #171 (b18775275_MS_990_0171.JP2)
Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0171.JP2#xywh=300,300,4920,6253
Summary:      Folio 208r of Wellcome MS.990 presents two columns of 17th-century German and Latin medical recipes and therapeutic instructions. The left column opens with a secret arcanum ('Ein schönes Arcana') prepared by distilling bryony root, cyclamen root, and white hellebore in water, administered in Malmsey wine via a small glass pipette (accompanied by an inline triangular symbol/sketch of the glass tip) to purge contagious poisons from the stomach, followed by a section attributed to 'H. Rönötten' on removing the cause of the illness through purgation, clysters, bloodletting, and especially sweating. The right column discusses sweating as a sure remedy for this and other fevers, warning against overheating ingredients (brandy, pepper, pellitory, castoreum, camphor, sulfur), debating whether camphor cools or heats, and providing several sudorific recipes (angelica root with theriac, elecampane in red wine, lovage root with wine vinegar, rue juice with theriac) as well as external warming methods using vinegar-moistened bricks, hot water flasks, and a vinegar-and-theriac compress applied over the navel.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen

Summary:      Page 201 (verso) in two columns. The upper left continues a regimen on managing sweat and preventing sleep in poisoned or feverish patients (including heart-strengthening cordials). The main section 'Vom Aderlasen' (Of Bloodletting) argues against bloodletting in this continuous fever because it weakens the body's moisture and drives heat toward the heart, brain, chest, or kidneys, followed by a red rubric noting that experience shows all who died had been bled. The right column concludes with remarks on aiding natural purgation (vomiting, suppositories, or laxative foods).

Summary:      Folio 228v opens the chapter 'Von Bluet speiben' (On Spitting of Blood / Hemoptysis) in two columns. The upper-left features a colored watercolor illustration of a woman vomiting/spitting blood into a bowl. The left column explains the causes, diagnostic distinctions (lung vs. chest vs. stomach vs. head bleeding), and prognosis of hemoptysis. The right column discusses fever-related risks, bloodletting (arm, hand, foot, and leeches to the hemorrhoidal vein), dietary regimen, and three remedies: turpentine/Indian balsam pills with China/sarsaparilla decoction, a 'wonderful electuary' of henbane, poppy, terra sigillata, and red coral, and a 'special remedy' of crab ashes dissolved in vinegar.

PAGE / FOLIO: 230 (verso) | IIIF Canvas #200 (b18775275_MS_990_0200.JP2)
Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0200.JP2#xywh=800,300,4630,6253
Summary:      Folio 230 verso from Wellcome Collection MS.990 (c. 1675), containing medical notes and recipes in Early New High German with Latin pharmaceutical terminology. The left column concludes a remedy for disordered blood (recommending rhubarb to draw water from the blood), followed by an ink-and-watercolor illustration of a patient inhaling medicinal vapors beneath a linen tent over a brazier. Below the illustration, a section titled 'Fluß Chatar' defines catarrh as phlegm and moisture rising from the stomach, spleen, liver, or womb into the head like vapors in an alembic, listing resulting ailments (apoplexy, abscesses, ear/eye/tooth pain, angina, suffocative catarrh, gout, sciatica). The right column continues the typology of cold and hot catarrhs, prescribes universal purges (emetics, Hauptpillen, syrups of betony, stoechas, calendula, sage, rosemary, violets, chicory), and provides two recipes in red-headed sections: a fumigation ('Volgenter Rauch Ist Köstlich') with white amber, mastic, cloves, and masterwort, and a medicated head fomentation/cap ('Bäthe auf das haubt für Catar... f. Scuffia') with hartshorn, barley, bran, marjoram, betony, red roses, Arabian stoechas, camel's hay, fennel, sweet flag, and mastic.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen

PAGE / FOLIO: 231 (recto) | IIIF Canvas #201 (b18775275_MS_990_0201.JP2)
Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0201.JP2#xywh=300,300,4871,6253
Summary:      Folio 231 recto from Wellcome MS.990 (c. 1675) presents German and Latin medical recipes and clinical commentary in two columns. The left column contains four fumigation (Rauch) recipes for hot and cold catarrhs and fluxes of the head, followed by an electuary and mutton-broth remedy for prolonged coughing and wheezing, and begins a section on hot catarrh (Von den Hitzigen Catarrn). The right column continues the treatment of hot catarrh—discussing bloodletting, a rhubarb-tamarind purgative, laudanum opiatum, and chest syrups (including coltsfoot), as well as hoarseness—before introducing a new major section on coughing (Von dem Huesten), detailing its physiology, causes (phlegm from the head, vapors from liver, stomach, spleen, or womb, and lung ulcers), and therapeutic cautions.

Tokens Used:  Input: 1,850 | Output: 2,650

Summary:      Page 261 (verso) continues the treatise on pulse diagnostics, cataloging the qualitative varieties of the pulse according to classical Galenic sphygmology: equal and unequal pulses, the recurrent pulse in the elderly, the intermittent/sawing ('verchlofne') pulse, the undulating wave-like ('wellende') pulse, the goat-leaping ('Caprisissa'), worm-like ('Wurmechtige / Vermicansa'), ant-like ('ameissige / formicansa') pulses—warning that the latter three portend death—as well as the trembling ('ziterte') pulse, the intercidens pulse in young healthy subjects, and weak pulses in malignant fevers.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Tokens Used:  Input: 1,290 | Output: 1,950

PAGE / FOLIO: 262 (recto) | IIIF Canvas #235 (b18775275_MS_990_0235.JP2)
Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0235.JP2#xywh=300,300,4861,6253
Summary:      Folio 262r continues a medical treatise on sphygmology (pulse diagnosis). It discusses the difficulty of recognizing the pulse, the proper comportment and technique of the physician when approaching the patient and taking the pulse (arm position, four-finger palpation, delicacy of hand, patient stillness and fasting, taking both hands, considering the patient's complexion and body heat), and variations of the pulse according to sex and age (men vs. women, elderly, youths, and children), concluding with an aphorism on the supreme importance of pulse knowledge.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Tokens Used:  Input: 2,850 | Output: 2,400

Summary:      Recto folio 292 opening the chapter on 'Melancolia. hipocontrica.' (Hypochondriac Melancholy). The upper left features a coloured ink-and-wash portrait of a melancholic man holding a staff and a celestial globe on a golden stand beside a four-paned window showing a starry night sky and crescent moon. The text describes the humoral etiology (burnt blood collecting in the mesenteric veins, affecting spleen, stomach, heart, and brain), physical symptoms (bloating, constipation, palpitations, dizziness, cold sweat), and behavioral manifestations (solitude, avoidance of company, devotion to reading and study).

Summary:      Recto folio 294, arranged in two columns, continuing the account of the effects of melancholia hypochondriaca. It details the patient's changeable appetite, strange delusions, hemorrhoids ('guldine ader'), progression to chronic illness with quartan fever, and the physician's predicament—receiving blame, ingratitude, and slander from obstinate patients who constantly complain and change doctors. It concludes by identifying the primary cause as sour, foul moisture in the stomach from poor digestion, exacerbated by salted/spiced meats, sedentary habits, and excessive nocturnal study.

Summary:      Surgical treatise 'Von fistlen in Gemain' (Of fistulas in general), accompanied by a watercolor illustration of a seated man with red lesions/fistulas on his face, arms, and legs. The text discusses probing fistulas to assess depth and hidden passages, widening openings with tent dilators (Stellmeißel), deciding between surgical excision/cauterization and palliative care near major nerves and blood vessels, and supporting local treatment with strict diet, purgatives, decoctions, and wound potions.

Summary:      Early New High German medical/apothecary manuscript (Wellcome MS.990, p. 565, verso). The left column concludes a treatment note and presents a rubricated section on the signs and diagnosis of fistulas (distinguishing marrow, nerve/membrane, flesh, blood-vessel, and carious-bone fistulas, followed by dietary and caustic treatment advice). The right column begins a rubricated section on fistulas of the breast/chest, followed by four Latin-German apothecary recipes: a precious plaster for fistulas with preparation instructions, two salves/liniments, and a caustic wash for spongy flesh in fistulas.

Summary:      Continuation of a medical treatise on syphilis (Franzosenkrankheit / Morbus Gallicus), detailing its symptoms (pustules, bone pains, ulceration of the uvula, tonsils, throat, and genitals, dark circles under the eyes, general weakness, and latency periods) and five methods of treatment: (1) the wood cure (guaiac, sassafras, sarsaparilla, China root), (2) purgation with mercurials (mercurius dulcis, arcanum corallinum, white precipitate, turpethum minerale), (3) the fumigation/smoke cure with cinnabar, (4) the inunction/ointment cure with mercury, and (5) bathing in mercurial sublimate water. The author concludes that among these five cures, the mercury inunction cure is the best and most reliable.
